passages.t: ‘This one was born in Zion’: the nations counted as citizens
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Psalm of the sons of Korah. A song” (verse 1). It is a short psalm about a city. “He has founded His city on the holy mountains” (verse 1). “The LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob” (verse 2). “Glorious things are ascribed to you, O city of God” (verse 3).

Then God speaks, and something surprising happens. He names nations that had been Israel's enemies and oppressors: “I will mention Rahab and Babylon among those who know Me” (verse 4), along with Philistia, Tyre and Cush. And of each he says, ‘This one was born in Zion.’

The psalm goes on. People from everywhere will be counted as Zion's own children (verse 5). “The LORD will record in the register of the peoples: ‘This one was born in Zion’” (verse 6).

It ends with music and dancing. “Singers and pipers will proclaim, ‘All my springs of joy are in You’” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
‘Rahab’ here is not the woman of Jericho. It is a poetic name for Egypt, taken from a sea monster. Isaiah calls Egypt “Rahab Who Sits Still” (Isaiah 30:7). So the list runs: Egypt, which enslaved Israel; Babylon, which would destroy Jerusalem; Philistia, the old rival on the coast; Tyre, the rich trading city; and Cush, the land far south of Egypt, at the edge of the world Israel knew.

Cities in the ancient world kept lists of their citizens. To be written in the register was to belong. In this psalm God himself writes the names, and he writes foreign names as if they were born in Jerusalem.

The Hebrew of verses 4 to 6 is short and hard to translate, and it is read in two main ways. Most Jewish and Christian readers take it to mean that people of the nations who come to know the LORD will be counted as full citizens of Zion. Others read it of Israelites scattered among those nations, whom God still counts as born in Zion. Both readings are held.
passages.later:
Isaiah saw the same hope: “Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance” (Isaiah 19:25).

Paul wrote, “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Galatians 4:26). And Revelation shows “a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne” (Revelation 7:9).
passages.asks:
Where were you born, and who are your people? Psalm 87 says that God can write a new birthplace beside your name. People who were once far off can be counted as his own.

This psalm speaks of God's city, not of any modern state or border. Let it soften the way you see people from other nations. God may be writing their names in his book.
